examDifficulty.heading: Is the Heroku Architect Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The Heroku Architect exam is hard. It rewards practical Salesforce experience because many questions ask you to choose the best configuration, design, or troubleshooting approach rather than recall isolated definitions.
bullets: ~68% passing score — build a margin above the minimum before booking.
Scenario-based choices — expect questions that test when to use Heroku, Scalability, or Deployment.
Hands-on context matters — candidates who have configured or supported Heroku in a real org are better prepared than candidates who only memorize notes.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Aim for 75%+ on timed practice sets before booking. If your score is below that, review the highest-weight topics first and retake questions until you can explain why each wrong option is wrong.

examFormat.heading: Heroku Architect Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The Heroku Architect exam is a timed Salesforce credential exam. Use the format below to plan pacing and practice-test strategy.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: A meaningful share of questions are scenario-based. The common pattern is a business requirement followed by several plausible Salesforce options; your job is to identify the safest, most maintainable choice for Heroku.
bestWayToPass: Start with the official outline: Map each exam objective to your notes, Trailhead practice, and weak areas before taking full mocks.
Prioritize high-impact topics: Spend extra time on Heroku, Scalability, and Deployment because these usually drive the hardest scenario questions.
Practice under time pressure: Use timed question sets so you learn when to move on and return to marked questions later.
Review explanations deeply: Do not just memorize the right option; write down why the other options are less appropriate for the scenario.

certificationCard.description: This exam tests enterprise-scale Heroku architecture — dyno sizing, Postgres configuration, Private Spaces, and CI/CD pipelines. You’ll need to know Heroku Connect patterns for Salesforce data sync and how to design for high availability.

keyConcepts.h2: Heroku Architect: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Heroku Platform Architecture & Dynos
blocks.body: Heroku runs applications in lightweight Linux containers called Dynos. Dyno types: Web (handles HTTP traffic), Worker (background jobs, no HTTP), One-Off (manual or scheduled tasks). Dyno sizes range from Eco (shared, sleeps after 30 min) to Performance-XL (dedicated, high memory). The Dyno Manager restarts crashed dynos automatically. Horizontal scaling adds more dynos of the same type; vertical scaling changes the dyno size. The Procfile defines process types and start commands. The Router load-balances requests across web dynos (round-robin with session stickiness disabled by default). The architect exam tests how to size and scale a Heroku deployment for a given traffic and processing profile.

blocks.heading: Data Services: Heroku Postgres & Redis
blocks.body: Heroku Postgres is the primary managed database — available in Essential (row limits), Standard, Premium, and Private tiers. Connection pooling via PgBouncer reduces database connection overhead. Follow databases provide read replicas for analytics queries. Continuous protection (WAL archiving) enables point-in-time recovery. Heroku Data for Redis handles caching, session storage, and pub/sub messaging. Redis plans: Mini (non-persistent) to Premium (persistent, HA). Heroku Key-Value Store (Redis) replaces legacy Heroku Redis. The exam tests data tier selection for a given durability, availability, and performance requirement, and how to configure read replicas for a high-read workload.

blocks.heading: CI/CD, Review Apps & Release Management
blocks.body: Heroku Pipelines define promotion stages: Development → Staging → Production. Review Apps automatically deploy pull requests to ephemeral apps for testing — each PR gets its own URL. Heroku CI runs automated tests on each push and blocks promotion on failure. The `heroku pipelines:promote` command promotes a slug (compiled app image) from one stage to the next without rebuilding. Release Phase runs migration scripts or data seeding commands before each new release goes live. Rollbacks revert to a previous release slug instantly. Config Vars (environment variables) are separate per stage, preventing accidental production config in staging. The exam tests how to design a pipeline for a team with multiple parallel feature branches.

blocks.heading: Security, Compliance & Private Spaces
blocks.body: Heroku Private Spaces run Dynos and data services inside a dedicated, isolated network environment — required for compliance workloads (HIPAA, PCI, SOC 2). Private Spaces connect to Salesforce orgs via Salesforce Private Connect (AWS PrivateLink) for secure data exchange without traffic traversing the public internet. Internal Routing restricts apps in a Private Space to only receive traffic from within the space. Shield Private Spaces add encryption at rest and enhanced security controls. Log Drains export Heroku logs to external SIEM or logging systems. Heroku Enterprise provides **SSO**, audit logs, and team-based access controls. The exam tests Private Space configuration for compliance scenarios and the networking model.

blocks.heading: Architecture Patterns for Salesforce + Heroku
blocks.body: Heroku Connect syncs data bidirectionally between Heroku Postgres and Salesforce objects — enabling Heroku apps to read/write Salesforce data without direct API calls. Write acceleration pattern: high-volume writes go to Heroku Postgres first, then Heroku Connect syncs to Salesforce asynchronously, avoiding API rate limits. Event-driven pattern: Salesforce **Platform Events** trigger Heroku workers via Heroku Connect CDC. Compute-offload pattern: complex calculations (ML inference, image processing) run on Heroku and results are written back to Salesforce. The architect exam tests which pattern to apply for a given scalability, latency, and Salesforce API limit scenario — especially for IoT, mobile, or high-volume data scenarios.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Heroku Architect Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The Heroku Architect exam tests enterprise-scale Heroku deployment design. Focus on Heroku infrastructure components, Heroku Connect for Salesforce data sync, high-availability patterns, and security architecture.

blocks.heading: Heroku Infrastructure Components
blocks.body: Know dynos (web, worker, one-off), formations, add-ons, buildpacks, and config vars. Understand how these components combine to run a scalable application on Heroku.

blocks.heading: Heroku Connect Architecture
blocks.body: Know how Heroku Connect syncs data between Heroku Postgres and Salesforce using polled sync (Salesforce → Postgres) and a Salesforce trigger (Postgres → Salesforce). Understand conflict resolution and sync frequency.

blocks.heading: High Availability & Scaling
blocks.body: Understand horizontal scaling (multiple dynos), how the Heroku Router load-balances requests, database connection pooling (PgBouncer), and how to design for zero-downtime deployments.

blocks.heading: Security Architecture
blocks.body: Know how to use Private Spaces for network isolation, Heroku Shield for HIPAA/PCI compliance, and how to secure data in transit (TLS) and at rest with encrypted Heroku Postgres.

blocks.heading: Performance Optimization
blocks.body: Know how to use Heroku caching (Redis add-on), async job processing (worker dynos with Sidekiq/Celery), and database query optimization to design performant Heroku applications.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Architect Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After this architect certification, progress toward CTA or other architect domains:

sampleQuestions.question: What does a Heroku Architect do?
options: Architect scalable solutions, deploy and manage apps, and manage teams and build-workflows on Heroku
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certified Heroku Architects are skilled at architecting scalable solutions, deploying and managing apps, and managing teams and build-workflows on Heroku.
whyWrong: 'Only coding' undersells the role, which spans architecture, deployment, and team/workflow management, not just code.
'Only reporting' misrepresents the role, which is about architecture and operations, not reporting.
'Only Slack' is unrelated to what a Heroku Architect actually does.

sampleQuestions.question: What is Heroku?
options: A cloud platform (PaaS) for building, running, and managing apps
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku is a cloud platform (PaaS) for building and running apps.
whyWrong: Heroku isn't a CRM — it's a platform-as-a-service for running applications.
Heroku isn't primarily an email tool — that's unrelated to its core PaaS function.
Heroku is more than just a database — it's a full platform for building and running apps.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a key activity for a Heroku Architect?
options: Architecting scalable solutions and managing deployment workflows
sampleQuestions.explanation: They architect scalable solutions and manage deployment workflows.
whyWrong: 'Only coding' undersells the key activity, which includes architecture and workflow management, not just writing code.
'Only reporting' misrepresents the key activity, which is about architecture and deployment, not reporting.
'Only lists' is unrelated to the actual key activity being described.

sampleQuestions.question: Which role typically pursues Heroku Architect?
options: Architects and senior developers working with Heroku
sampleQuestions.explanation: Architects and senior developers working with Heroku pursue this credential.
whyWrong: Marketers aren't the typical audience for this platform architecture credential.
Sales roles aren't the typical audience for this technical architecture credential.
Designers aren't the typical audience — this targets architects and senior developers.

sampleQuestions.question: What does 'build-workflows' mean in Heroku context?
options: CI/CD, pipelines, and release management on Heroku
sampleQuestions.explanation: Build-workflows include CI/CD, pipelines, and release management on Heroku.
whyWrong: 'Only CI' undersells build-workflows, which include CD and release management too.
'Only CD' undersells build-workflows, which include CI and release management too.
'Only testing' undersells build-workflows, which is broader than testing alone.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a Heroku Dyno?
options: A lightweight container that runs application code
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dynos are containers that run app processes on Heroku.
whyWrong: A Dyno isn't a database — that's a separate Heroku Postgres service.
A Dyno isn't an email service — that's unrelated to its function.
A Dyno isn't a storage bucket — it's a lightweight compute container.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku feature supports horizontal scaling?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku supports scaling web and worker dynos horizontally.
whyWrong: 'Single dyno only' is the opposite of what horizontal scaling provides.
'No scaling' contradicts the fact that dyno scaling is a real, core Heroku capability.
'Vertical only' misrepresents dyno scaling, which is specifically about horizontal (multiple dyno) scaling.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Heroku Postgres provide?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Heroku Postgres is a managed database add-on.
whyWrong: 'Only backups' undersells Heroku Postgres, which is a full managed relational database service, not just backups.
'No database' contradicts the fact that Heroku Postgres is a real managed database offering.
'External only' misrepresents Heroku Postgres as an external-only service when it's a native Heroku offering.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku feature manages environment-specific configuration?
whyWrong: Hardcoded values are the opposite of what Config Vars are designed to replace.
'Only buildpacks' misattributes environment configuration to a different Heroku feature.
'Only releases' misattributes environment configuration to a different Heroku feature.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a Heroku buildpack?
options: Scripts that compile and prepare an app for execution
sampleQuestions.explanation: Buildpacks compile and prepare apps for the dyno environment.
whyWrong: A buildpack isn't a database — that's a separate Heroku Postgres service.
A buildpack isn't just an add-on — it's core to how an app is compiled and prepared for execution.
A buildpack isn't a dyno type — dynos run the app after buildpacks prepare it.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku feature supports zero-downtime deployments?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Preboot and release phase enable zero-downtime deployments.
whyWrong: 'No support' contradicts the fact that Heroku explicitly supports zero-downtime deployment mechanisms.
'Manual only' contradicts the fact that preboot and release phase are automated features.
'Single dyno only' misrepresents the multi-dyno mechanism that enables zero-downtime deploys.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Heroku Pipelines support?
whyWrong: 'Only staging' undersells Pipelines, which support the full dev-to-production workflow, not just staging.
'Production only' undersells Pipelines, which manage the full multi-stage workflow, not just production.
'No staging' contradicts the fact that Pipelines explicitly support staging as part of the workflow.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Heroku add-on category supports background jobs?
options: Worker dynos and queue add-ons (e.g., Redis)
sampleQuestions.explanation: Worker dynos and queues support background job processing.
whyWrong: Database add-ons don't provide background job/queue functionality — that's a separate category.
Email add-ons are unrelated to background job processing.
Storage add-ons are unrelated to background job processing.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of Heroku Review Apps?
options: Automatic ephemeral apps for pull request review
sampleQuestions.explanation: Review Apps create ephemeral apps for PR review.
whyWrong: Production apps aren't the ephemeral review apps described — those are for PR review specifically.
'Staging only' misrepresents Review Apps, which are created automatically for pull requests, not just staging.
'No automation' contradicts the fact that Review Apps are specifically an automated feature.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best practice applies to Heroku architecture?
options: Design for stateless processes, use 12-factor app methodology
sampleQuestions.explanation: Stateless processes and 12-factor methodology support scalability.
whyWrong: Ignoring scaling contradicts a core best practice for cloud-native Heroku architecture.
'Single dyno only' contradicts the scalable, multi-dyno design best practice recommends.
'No logging' contradicts the fact that logging is part of sound 12-factor app design.
